findings.description: The reports_archive bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects are stored with S3's default (SSE-S3 or unencrypted depending on account defaults) at best and no customer-managed KMS key is enforced. This bucket also holds the vendor-roster object, so sensitive vendor data may be written without the organization's KMS key policy controlling access.

The ledger_exports bucket contains no server_side_encryption_configuration, so financial ledger exports are stored without enforced encryption using a controlled KMS key. Anyone with read access to the underlying storage or an unencrypted snapshot can read the data.
The model_artifacts bucket has versioning and logging but no server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving model artifacts unprotected by an enforced KMS key at rest.

The ops_runbooks bucket is configured without any server_side_encryption_configuration, so operational runbooks (which frequently contain internal credentials and procedures) are stored without enforced encryption.

The audit_trail bucket is created with acl = "log-delivery-write", which grants the S3 log delivery group WRITE and READ_ACP on the bucket. This bucket is the security audit log sink; allowing a shared log-delivery group to write to it means an attacker controlling log delivery can inject or manipulate audit records, undermining the integrity of the audit trail.

The vendor-roster object uploaded into reports_archive specifies no server-side encryption (no server_side_encryption or kms_key_id), so the spreadsheet of vendor PII is written to a bucket that itself has no default encryption configuration.
